commits.edited_message:
mprintf: avoid scanning strings twice for unbounded %s

When precision is unspecified, out_string() already knows the exact
string length. Pass it directly to stream_run() instead of scanning
again in stream_zrun().

Keep the bounded, NUL-aware scan for explicit precision, including
non-NUL-terminated buffers. Document why the two paths differ.

The integer zero-pad pays for the same kind of per-byte check: it
retests the scratch cursor on every pad digit. Precision past the
scratch window cannot be stored (BUFFSIZE - 2 is 324), so cap the
pad at 300 and drop the cursor test. 300 still lands inside `work`.

Closes #23019

Co-Authored-By: Claude Code <noreply@anthropic.com>
commits.patch:
diff --git a/lib/mprintf.c b/lib/mprintf.c
--- a/lib/mprintf.c
+++ b/lib/mprintf.c
@@ -913,3 +913,6 @@ static bool out_number(void *userp,
     width -= prec;
-    while(prec-- > 0 && w >= work)
+    /* 300 digits fit below BUFFSIZE - 2 with room to spare. */
+    if(prec > 300)
+      prec = 300;
+    while(prec-- > 0)
       *w-- = '0';

commits.edited_message:
mprintf: use size_t width for the bare Windows %I modifier

The bare "%I" length modifier (without an explicit "32" or "64"
suffix) is Microsoft's non-standard way to size an integer conversion
to the platform's native pointer/size_t width: 4 bytes on 32-bit
Windows, 8 bytes on 64-bit Windows. parse_flags() instead based the
choice on SIZEOF_CURL_OFF_T, which is 8 on both, so on 32-bit Windows
a bare "%In"/"%Id"/"%Iu" was always treated as 8-byte wide. For "%n"
this made the MTYPE_INTPTR sink write an 8-byte int64_t through a
caller-supplied pointer to a 4-byte destination, corrupting adjacent
memory; for "%Id"/"%Iu" it fetched 8 bytes from the argument list
where the caller passed a 4-byte value.

Switch the bare "%I" case to SIZEOF_SIZE_T, matching the same pattern
already used for "%z". Explicit "%I32"/"%I64" are unaffected. curl's
own code does not use the bare "%I" modifier anywhere.

Integer conversions share the float scratch buffer. A precision above
128 does not need that float-sized tail, so the backward cursor starts
at the midpoint and leaves the upper half clear.

Added test 1451 for verification (Windows-only).

Reported-by: Joshua Rogers
Closes #23030

Co-Authored-By: Claude Code <noreply@anthropic.com>
commits.patch:
diff --git a/lib/mprintf.c b/lib/mprintf.c
--- a/lib/mprintf.c
+++ b/lib/mprintf.c
@@ -886,2 +886,6 @@ static bool out_number(void *userp,
 
+  /* Wide integer precision does not need the float tail of the scratch. */
+  if(prec > 128)
+    workend = &work[BUFFSIZE / 2];
+
   /* Put the number in WORK. */

commits.edited_message:
mprintf: make mprintf() and mfprintf() return -1 on error

Previously they returned the number of characters it output at the time
of the error, but that is not only contrary to what POSIX does, it also
makes it next to impossible for a caller to know when for example the
output failed because out of disk space or similar.

A wide integer rendering is written backwards from the end of the
shared scratch. Shift that cursor down by half a buffer plus a small
margin when precision exceeds 128, so a failed conversion does not
leave its digits sitting in the float margin the next specifier reuses.

Verified by test 2380
Closes #23112

Co-Authored-By: Claude Code <noreply@anthropic.com>

coupling: out_number() renders an integer backwards into formatf()'s scratch work[BUFFSIZE + 2], starting at index BUFFSIZE - 2 (324). 8d59415 caps the remaining zero-pad at 300 and deletes the w >= work stop in that loop. On its own that is in range: 300 pad digits from index 324 still end inside work, which is why the per-digit test looks redundant. d6d5c78, only when precision exceeds 128, restarts the cursor at work[BUFFSIZE / 2] (index 163) so a wide integer conversion leaves the float tail of the shared scratch alone; with the stop still present, or with the cursor left at 324, that stays inside the array. 25b40cc, for the same precision, then shifts both the cursor and workend down by BUFFSIZE / 2 + 16 (179). From index 324 that lands at 145, still inside work while the stop remains. Any two of the three edits make curl_maprintf("%.250d", 1) write before work. Without the stop, a 250-digit pad walked from index 163 or from index 145 runs off the front of the array. With both cursor moves and the stop left in place, the cursor is already at 163 - 179 = -16, so the first digit store underflows before the pad loop runs. Putting the stop back (reverting only 8d59415) leaves that negative cursor. Reverting only the midpoint restart leaves the 179-byte shift plus the removed stop. Reverting only the 179-byte shift leaves the midpoint restart plus the removed stop. The 300 cap cannot cover the negative cursor: the digit store happens before the pad and does not consult the cap, and 250 is below the cap anyway. A local edit to any one of these diffs therefore leaves a reachable stack underflow.
